meta.titre: Prepositions: time, place and the words that need a fixed partner

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A taxi driver in Yaounde says *I am waiting for the passengers*, *I have driven since morning* and *I depend on the early customers*. Every little word before the noun matters: change *for* to *to*, or *since* to *for*, and the sentence becomes wrong. Prepositions are small, but the grammar section of Paper 1 tests them every year, because they must be learnt in the right combinations. This course gives you the rules that cover most questions and a method for the rest.

items: A noun names a person, a place or a thing, and a pronoun replaces a noun (*him, it, them*).
The present perfect is formed with *have* or *has* + past participle (*has lived*).
The -ing form of a verb can be used like a noun (*Swimming is fun*).

sections.titre: Prepositions of time, place and fixed combinations
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a preposition does

A preposition links a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form to the rest of the sentence. After a preposition use a noun, a pronoun or the **-ing** form: *good at swimming*, not *good at swim*.

### Time

| Preposition | Use | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| at | a clock time or a point | at 6 o'clock, at noon, at night |
| on | days and dates | on Monday, on 5 May |
| in | months, years, seasons, parts of the day | in July, in 2020, in the evening |
| since | the starting point (with a perfect tense) | since 2018, since Monday |
| for | the length of time | for three years, for two hours |
| by | not later than | finish the work by Friday |
| until | up to that time | wait until six |
| during | within a period (followed by a noun) | during the holidays |

### Place and movement

- **at** a point (*at the bus stop*), **in** a closed space or a large area (*in the room, in Kumba*), **on** a surface (*on the table*).
- **between** two things; **among** three or more (*among the trees*).
- Movement: **to, from, into, out of, across, through, along, towards**.

### Fixed (dependent) combinations

Some verbs and adjectives must be followed by a particular preposition. Learn them in pairs.

| Verbs | Adjectives |
|---|---|
| depend on, rely on, listen to, wait for, look for, laugh at, believe in, belong to, suffer from, apologise to (a person) for (a fault) | afraid of, proud of, good at, interested in, tired of, different from, responsible for, angry with (a person) |

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a perfect tense is used with a time expression
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use **since** with a point in time (*since Monday, since 2018, since I was a child*) and **for** with a length of time (*for two days, for ten years*). Both are common with the present perfect: *She has lived here since 2015* and *She has lived here for ten years*.

variantes.nom: Fixed combinations with verbs and adjectives
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the word before the gap is a verb or an adjective that needs a particular preposition
variantes.contenu_markdown: The word before the gap decides the answer. Learn the pairs from your reading. If the preposition is followed by a verb, use the -ing form: *tired of waiting*. The word *to* is a preposition in *look forward to*, so the next verb is -ing: *I look forward to seeing you*.

First ask what the gap is for: a time, a place, or a link with a verb or adjective. Then read the word before the gap and the word after it. Say the sentence with each option and remove those that clash with the rules above. If two options remain, think of a similar sentence that you know is correct.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct preposition for each gap.

*My uncle has worked in this hospital \_\_\_\_\_\_ ten years, and he is proud \_\_\_\_\_\_ his work.*

(a) first gap: (A) since (B) for (C) at (D) in

(b) second gap: (A) for (B) at (C) of (D) to

etapes.justification: The tense is the present perfect and the words after the gap, *ten years*, give a length of time, not a starting point.

etapes.action: Check the first gap with the other options.
etapes.justification: *at* is used for a point in time and *in* for a month or a year, so they do not fit before *ten years*.
The word before the gap is the adjective *proud*, which is always followed by *of*.

etapes.action: Test the other options for the second gap.
etapes.justification: *proud for*, *proud at* and *proud to* are not the normal combinations.
Reading it aloud confirms that both choices are natural.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *My uncle has worked in this hospital for ten years, and he is proud of his work.*

sections.conclusion_markdown: The answers are **(a) for** and **(b) of**. The tense and the words after the gap decide a time preposition, while the word before the gap decides a fixed combination.

items.erreur_markdown: "I have lived here since five years." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: *Five years* is a length of time, so *for* is needed. *Since* needs a starting point.
items.correction_markdown: I have lived here **for** five years.

items.erreur_markdown: "She is married with a teacher." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: The correct pair is *married to* a person.

items.erreur_markdown: "He depends of his uncle." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: The verb *depend* is followed by *on*, not *of*.

items.erreur_markdown: "We arrived to Douala at night." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: With a town or a country we say *arrive in*, and with a smaller place such as a station or a school we say *arrive at*. *Arrive to* is not used.

items.erreur_markdown: "I am waiting you at the gate." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: The verb *wait* needs the preposition *for* before its object.
items.correction_markdown: I am waiting **for** you at the gate.

items.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct preposition.

(a) The meeting starts \_\_\_\_\_\_ 9 o'clock. (at / on / in)

(b) Her birthday is \_\_\_\_\_\_ 14 March. (at / on / in)

(c) We have lived here \_\_\_\_\_\_ 2015. (since / for / at)

(d) The cat is hiding \_\_\_\_\_\_ the table. (under / to / since)

Choose from the words in brackets.

(a) She is good \_\_\_\_\_\_ solving puzzles. (at / in / on)

(b) He apologised \_\_\_\_\_\_ the teacher \_\_\_\_\_\_ being late. (first gap: to / for / with; second gap: for / of / at)

(c) The farmer shared the land \_\_\_\_\_\_ his three sons. (between / among / to)

(d) The swimmer swam \_\_\_\_\_\_ the river and reached the other side. (across / under / along)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **at** (*good at* + -ing).

(b) **to**, then **for** (*apologise to* a person *for* a fault).

(c) **among** (more than two people).

(d) **across** (from one side to the other).

items.enonce_markdown:
Each sentence has one mistake with a preposition. Rewrite the sentence correctly.

(a) She is interested on learning French.

(b) We are looking forward to see you.

(c) He has been ill since three days.

(d) He is afraid from snakes.

(e) The pupils listened carefully the teacher.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) She is interested **in** learning French.

(b) We are looking forward to **seeing** you (*to* is a preposition, so -ing follows).

(c) He has been ill **for** three days (a length of time).

(d) He is afraid **of** snakes.

(e) The pupils listened carefully **to** the teacher.

items_markdown: Use at for a clock time, on for days and dates, and in for months, years, seasons and parts of the day.
Since goes with a starting point and for with a length of time.
Use between for two and among for more than two.
Learn fixed pairs such as depend on, listen to, wait for, afraid of, proud of, good at.
After a preposition, use a noun, a pronoun or the -ing form.
In a gap question, look at the word before and the word after the gap, then test each option.
